prompt: Each situation reflects one of Hofstede's dimensions of national culture. Name the dimension it shows most clearly.

cases.text: In one country, employees rarely question a manager's decision, and shoppers trust a brand more when a senior executive endorses it.
cases.explanation: Power distance measures the extent to which less powerful members of a society accept and expect unequal distributions of authority and status hierarchy.

cases.text: Shoppers stick to familiar brands, read every formal guarantee, and avoid ambiguous products that have just come on the market.
cases.explanation: Uncertainty avoidance measures how strongly members of a culture feel threatened by ambiguous situations and seek formal rules, guarantees, and familiar brands.

cases.text: Automobile ads in one market show the driver beating rivals and finishing first. In another market, ads show a calm family enjoying quality of life on a weekend trip.
cases.explanation: Masculinity versus femininity contrasts societies emphasizing competition and material achievement against those emphasizing care and quality of life.

cases.text: Parents put a large share of their income into a long-term savings plan for their children's future education, even if it means fewer treats today.
cases.explanation: Long-term orientation measures emphasis on thrift, perseverance, and future rewards.

cases.text: A young buyer will not choose a new phone until parents and siblings have agreed on the brand that best preserves family harmony.
cases.explanation: Individualism versus collectivism contrasts personal autonomy and self-expression against harmony, duty, and in-group loyalty.

cases.text: A clothing brand's slogan invites customers to express personal autonomy and create a look that no one else has.
cases.explanation: Standing out through personal autonomy and self-expression reflects an individualist value system.

prompt: Identify which ritual type or gift-giving stage from Rook (1985), Sherry (1983), and van Gennep (1960) each consumer situation illustrates.

cases.text: Every morning before a client meeting, Tom applies cleanser, serum, and moisturizer in the exact same sequence before putting on his watch.
cases.explanation: Grooming rituals transition the individual from the private self to the public social self through a fixed sequence of behaviors.

cases.text: Two weeks before her sister's birthday, Nadia researches artisanal bookstores and buys a first-edition novel to have it gift-wrapped.
cases.explanation: In Sherry's (1983) model, gestation is the stage of selecting and purchasing the gift prior to the exchange.

cases.text: At the dinner table, Nadia hands the wrapped package to her sister while the family watches her open the ribbon and read the card.
cases.explanation: Presentation is the ceremonial exchange moment in which the gift is handed over and opened in front of the ritual audience.

cases.text: After exchanging thoughtful anniversary gifts, a couple feels a renewed sense of closeness and mutual appreciation.
cases.explanation: Reformulation is the final stage of gift-giving in which the relationship bond between giver and recipient is adjusted afterward.

cases.text: Upon completing university and starting her first professional job, Lea buys a tailored suit and celebrates with a graduation dinner.
cases.explanation: Rites of passage mark transitions between social statuses, such as graduation, marriage, parenthood, or retirement.

cases.text: Colleagues purchase a commemorative watch and host a farewell banquet when Maria retires after thirty years at the firm.
cases.explanation: Retirement is a rite of passage marking a major transition in social status accompanied by symbolic ritual artifacts.

prompt: Using Belk, Wallendorf, and Sherry's (1989) framework, identify whether each case represents profane consumption, sacred consumption, sacralization, or desacralization.

cases.text: Ahmed buys a standard bottle of unscented dish soap every two weeks for routine kitchen cleaning.
cases.explanation: Profane consumption involves ordinary, everyday utilitarian objects and routines that carry no special reverence.

cases.text: Lina frames the paper concert ticket from the night her partner proposed and hangs it in a protected display case.
cases.explanation: Sacralization occurs when an ordinary item becomes sacred through association with a deeply meaningful event, person, or collection.

cases.text: A revered religious symbol is mass-produced on $1.99 plastic party cups and disposable flip-flops in a bargain bin.
cases.explanation: Desacralization occurs when a formerly sacred symbol or holiday is mass-produced and commercialized into an ordinary commodity.

cases.text: Carlos keeps his late grandfather's pocket watch on a velvet stand in a locked cabinet and refuses to sell it at any price.
cases.explanation: Sacred consumption involves possessions set apart from the ordinary world and treated with awe, respect, and emotional protection.

cases.text: An office stapler sits in a shared supply drawer where coworkers use it without giving it a second thought.
cases.explanation: An everyday utilitarian tool with no emotional reverence belongs to the profane domain.

cases.text: An ordinary basketball jersey becomes a fan's most treasured possession after the team captain wears and signs it at a championship game.
cases.explanation: Sacralization through contamination occurs when an ordinary item becomes sacred by touching a revered person.

prompt: Sort each consumer behavior observation into a generational cohort effect, a life-stage effect, or bidirectional intergenerational household influence.

cards.text: Consumers who entered the job market during a severe macroeconomic downturn maintain a lifelong preference for low-debt living decades later.
cards.explanation: Lasting values formed by macroeconomic events experienced during youth represent a generational cohort effect.

cards.text: A couple in their early thirties shifts spending from late-night concerts to infant car seats and organic baby food after their first child is born.
cards.explanation: Changes in consumption caused by marriage, parenthood, or aging reflect a life-stage effect rather than a permanent generational trait.

cards.text: A university student moving into a first apartment buys the exact peanut butter and laundry detergent brands her parents always stocked at home.
cards.explanation: Parents socializing children into staple household grocery brands is an example of upward-to-downward intergenerational influence.

cards.text: A twenty-year-old college student teaches her parents which mobile banking app and noise-canceling headphones to adopt.
cards.explanation: Young adults guiding parents' adoption of digital apps and electronics illustrates reverse intergenerational influence within the household.

cards.text: Shoppers who grew up with smartphones in school continue to expect short-form video product discovery as they enter middle age.
cards.explanation: Formative technological habits acquired in youth that persist across the lifespan reflect a generational cohort effect.

cards.text: Upon retiring at age sixty-five, a homeowner sells a four-bedroom suburban house and purchases travel packages and health supplements.
cards.explanation: Adjusting spending patterns in response to retirement and aging is a life-stage effect.

question_text: Two wealthy shoppers purchase cashmere coats from the same luxury fashion house. Shopper A selects a coat with the brand's oversized monogram printed across the chest so anyone on the street recognizes its price. Shopper B pays a higher price for an unbranded coat whose hand-stitched lapel is recognized only by fellow connoisseurs. In Han, Nunes, and Drèze's (2010) taxonomy, how are Shopper A and Shopper B classified?
hint: Compare high-wealth consumers with a high need for status (loud logos) against high-wealth consumers with a low need for status (quiet luxury).
correct_answer_citation: Week 11: Conspicuous Consumption, Quiet Luxury, and Status Signaling (Han, Nunes, & Drèze, 2010)

options.option_text: Both shoppers are patricians, because both have high financial wealth
options.option_explanation: Han, Nunes, and Drèze (2010) separate wealthy consumers by their need for status and preference for brand prominence.

options.option_text: Shopper A is a patrician seeking quiet luxury, and Shopper B is a parvenu seeking loud conspicuous display
options.option_explanation: This reverses the two groups: parvenus prefer loud, visible logos whereas patricians prefer inconspicuous quiet luxury.

options.option_text: Shopper A is a parvenu using loud brand prominence to signal wealth broadly, and Shopper B is a patrician using quiet luxury recognized by fellow insiders
options.option_explanation: Correct. Parvenus (high wealth, high need for status) prefer prominent logos, whereas patricians (high wealth, low need for status) pay a premium for quiet luxury recognized by insiders with high cultural capital.

options.option_text: Shopper B is avoiding status signaling entirely because unbranded goods carry zero cultural capital
options.option_explanation: Patricians still signal status, but horizontally to fellow insiders possessing the cultural capital to recognize subtle craftsmanship.

prompt: Does each case illustrate a cognitive country-of-origin (COO) quality inference (Bilkey & Nes, 1982) or normative consumer ethnocentrism (Shimp & Sharma, 1987)?

cards.text: Ana infers that an unfamiliar handbag brand uses superior leather craftsmanship because the label states it was made in Italy.
cards.explanation: She uses a favorable country-category stereotype as an extrinsic cue to infer product quality.

cards.text: Ben buys a domestically manufactured appliance even though an imported model is rated higher, because he believes buying imports costs local workers their jobs.
cards.explanation: Consumer ethnocentrism is a normative moral belief that purchasing foreign-made goods harms the domestic economy.

cards.text: A buyer expects a new mechanical timepiece to keep accurate time because it carries a Swiss Made movement certification.
cards.explanation: The country of manufacture serves as a cognitive quality signal in a category linked with that nation.

cards.text: Chloe feels unpatriotic whenever she puts imported produce into her grocery cart and actively checks labels for domestic origin.
cards.explanation: Viewing foreign purchases as unpatriotic reflects high consumer ethnocentrism.

cards.text: A studio engineer assumes an unfamiliar audio interface will be reliable because it was engineered in Japan.
cards.explanation: Favorable country-category associations transfer positive quality expectations to unfamiliar brands from that nation.

cards.text: Dev strongly endorses the CETSCALE statement that citizens should always buy domestic products instead of imports.
cards.explanation: Shimp and Sharma's (1987) CETSCALE measures normative consumer ethnocentrism tendencies.

question_text: When Wadi, Ghodrat, and Philp (2026) administered the 17-item CETSCALE to frontier AI models developed in the United States, China, Canada, and France across prompts framed for consumers in each of those four countries, what pattern emerged across all tested models?
hint: Recall both the developer baseline finding and how CETSCALE scores shifted depending on which target country was named in the statements.
correct_answer_citation: Week 11: Measuring Consumer Ethnocentrism Across Frontier AI Models (Wadi, Ghodrat, & Philp, 2026)

options.option_text: All AI models produced identical CETSCALE scores regardless of developer origin or the target country named in the prompt
options.option_explanation: Models differed significantly in baseline ethnocentrism across developers and shifted systematically with the target country.

options.option_text: Models differed significantly in baseline ethnocentrism across developers, and across all models responses were consistently least ethnocentric when statements referred to China and significantly more ethnocentric when statements referred to the United States or Canada
options.option_explanation: Correct. Both developer baseline differences and the target-country shift (lowest for China, higher for the United States and Canada) emerged systematically.

options.option_text: Responses were most ethnocentric when statements referred to China and least ethnocentric when statements referred to Canada
options.option_explanation: The study found the opposite target-country pattern: responses were least ethnocentric when statements referred to China and significantly more ethnocentric for the United States or Canada.

options.option_text: Only models developed in the United States showed any variation across target countries
options.option_explanation: The target-country shift appeared across all tested models regardless of developer origin.
